Let's dive into Chapter 6: Working with Triggers in Everyday Life.
You know those days when it feels like the world is just full of hidden traps? Moments that seem small on the surface, but somehow, they set off a wave of frustration or hurt. Maybe it's your neighbor cranking up music late at night, your partner zoning out at dinner, or even a stranger tossing out a careless remark while you’re in the checkout line.
These are the everyday triggers—the little hooks that so easily pull us back into old patterns of anger or resentment.
Let me tell you about one woman’s story. For her, the trigger was that daily morning commute. Every single day, she’d find herself gripping the steering wheel, heart pounding, as other drivers cut her off or ignored the rules completely. The anger would build up, and by the time she got to work, it just spilled over into the rest of her day. She tried blasting music or tuning into podcasts, but that irritation just stuck around.
One morning, though, she decided to try something different. When that familiar surge of anger hit, she paused. She noticed the tightness in her body, the racing thoughts in her mind. And instead of reacting, she took a slow breath and gently reminded herself, “This is just a moment. I don’t have to bite the hook.”
Now, the anger didn’t magically disappear, but it wasn’t as sharp. She got to work feeling lighter, more present.
Most people don’t realize just how much power they have in these ordinary moments. The world? It’s always going to throw triggers our way—noisy neighbors, tricky coworkers, those unexpected setbacks. But here’s something to pay attention to: every trigger is also an invitation. It’s a chance to notice the hook, pause, and choose a different response.
There’s another story—a father who used to get completely overwhelmed by his child’s tantrums. He’d end up raising his voice, then feeling guilty for hours afterward. But with time, he started to see the tantrum for what it really was: a trigger, not a threat. When the yelling started, he’d pause, feel his own discomfort, and remind himself that both of them were struggling. That urge to snap back softened, and in its place, he found a sense of connection.
What becomes clear is that triggers aren’t the enemy. In fact, they’re opportunities—chances to practice awareness, to notice old patterns in action, and to choose a new way forward. The more we work with our triggers, the less power they have over us. Life shifts from trying to avoid discomfort to actually meeting each moment with curiosity and care.
And you know, this isn’t about becoming immune to frustration or pain. It’s really about building resilience—learning to stay present, even when things get hard. With time, those hooks just don’t feel as sharp, and your heart? It grows stronger.
